title: Predicting the Emergence of Induction Heads in Language Model Pretraining
claim: Distinct capabilities emerge abruptly at a specific training point, with sharp transitions rather than gradual improvement across metrics.
layout: 1 panel, dual y-axes, log-scaled x-axis, four metric curves with legend
description: A single line plot with a log-scaled x-axis, '# Tokens (log10)', running from 10^2 to about 5x10^5. The left y-axis shows accuracy from 0 to 0.8 for PS, LA and AR. The right y-axis shows AR mean rank from 0 to 20k. Four series have distinct markers and colors. Best PS is navy circles, Best LA is teal squares, AR accuracy is green triangles, and AR mean rank is a red dotted line with diamonds. All metrics stay flat until about 5x10^3 tokens. Then PS rises sharply to about 0.9. LA rises modestly to about 0.18. AR accuracy climbs later to about 0.3. Mean rank falls from about 25k toward 0. A legend box sits in the middle left, over the plot. The eye goes first to the steep navy PS rise and the red rank drop crossing it.
caption: Developmental trajectories of PS, LA, AR accuracy, and AR mean rank. The first three metrics are plotted in the scale on the left y-axis, and the last metric in the scale on the right y-axis.
abstract: Specialized attention heads dubbed induction heads (IHs) have been argued to underlie the remarkable in-context learning capabilities of modern language models; yet, a precise characterization of their emergence, especially in the context of language modeling, remains wanting. In this study, we investigate the relationship between statistical properties of the training data and IH formation in both natural and synthetic training data settings. We show that: (1) a simple equation combining batch size and context size predicts the point at which IHs form and that this emergence point is agnostic to model size; (2) surface bigram repetition frequency and reliability strongly affect the formation of IHs, and we find an effective decision boundary in terms of these two values; (3) local dependency with high bigram repetition frequency and reliability is sufficient for IH formation, but categoriality and the shape of the marginal distribution appear to modulate IH formation near the decision boundary.
